rationale.governing_rule: Owner's own standing rule, work_orders/drop/wo-20260902T194500.json: 'default to single-daemon extension unless isolation clearly wins.' The burden of proof is on each ADDITIONAL process.
rationale.charter_violation: README.md: 'Fully multithread capable by design. Concurrency is a property of the scheduler, not a flag on a script.' The 26-clock fleet makes concurrency a property of PROCESS COUNT. That is an architectural regression against a written requirement.
isolation_wins_twice: A supervisor may not share a fault domain with what it restarts. Health --supervise is the only in-tree restarter of Core :8770.

An executor of foreign work may not share a fault domain with the observer that reports on it. A wedged 1800s child would otherwise mute the heartbeat, and the fleet would report dead when it is merely busy.
rationale.unit_of_concurrency: A resident Python process is not the unit of concurrency; the child process is. Lane work is Popen+wait (I/O, not CPU), so the GIL is irrelevant and threads suffice. You do not need five interpreters to run five subprocesses.
rationale.cadence_rule: cadence >= 60s -> calendar --once. cadence < 60s -> a tick inside a resident process. Unbounded duration -> a job on the queue, never a clock.
rationale.runtime_binding_hazard: README.md names 'a scheduler executing eight-day-old code' as a founding failure. Every resident loop is pinned to the source on disk at logon; a --once task re-reads source on every fire and cannot execute stale code. P1/P2/P3 must therefore carry a version stamp and self-restart on source-hash change, or the collapse trades 14 small runtime-binding hazards for 3 large ones.

logon_relaunches.reason: ONLOGON is not supervision. It fires once at logon and never again, so a 03:00 crash stays dead until the next logon. Worse, a relaunch landing on a surviving process gives two claimers on one surface. One entry for P1; P1 starts and restarts P2/P3.

cdeck_glob.breaks: SILENTLY, which is the dangerous kind. A glob is count-free and order-free: it cannot distinguish 'peer X is missing' from 'peer X was never there.' Combined with staleness measured on the feed's own age, a fleet that lost eleven processes still shows green.

collapse_order.invariant: At all times, at least one live process is able to restart Core :8770, and Core itself is never stopped. Two restarters is a recoverable condition. Zero restarters, even for one step, is not.
collapse_order.rollback: schtasks /change /tn "<name>" /enable and start the old loop. Because nothing is ever deleted, every step is reversible — which is why /disable is worth the extra audit noise.

steps.step: Collapse the executors, ONE CLAIM SURFACE AT A TIME. Per surface: P3 takes the lease -> the old daemon's next claim refuses HELD -> stop the old daemon -> /disable its entry -> confirm the surface still drains. Order: critique, buckets, dispatch, work_order, queue. Lowest blast radius first.

steps.step: live/queue specifically — the double-claimed one. Retire cosmos_pool's claim FIRST, confirm cosmos_run still drains ALONE, THEN move the lane to P3, THEN retire cosmos_run. Never both at once, or you cannot tell which one was doing the work.

steps.step: Flip the readers, then drop the shims. Update PEER_HEARTBEATS / REQUIRED_DAEMONS / anti_loss_daemons to the new roster. PROVE EACH CAN STILL GO RED by inducing a failure. Only then stop writing the legacy shim names.

steps.step: Retire the deck's glob. Point cDeck at Core /api/v1. Last, because it is the observation surface.
